title: Remove All Adjacent Duplicates In String
description: Brute force to optimized: repeatedly rescanning and removing versus a single stack pass that automatically resolves cascading cancellations.

content.title: Remove All Adjacent Duplicates In String

blocks.text: You are given a string s consisting of lowercase English letters. A "duplicate removal" consists of choosing two ADJACENT and EQUAL letters and removing them. Repeat this process on s until no more duplicate removals can be made. Return the final resulting string, which is guaranteed to be unique.

blocks.caption: A stack directly simulates this: pushing each character, but popping (cancelling) instead when it matches the current top

blocks.text: Whenever two IDENTICAL letters sit directly next to each other, they cancel out entirely; this can then bring together two OTHER letters that were previously separated by the cancelled pair, potentially triggering further cancellations, and so on, until no adjacent pair remains equal.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Row of Dominoes That Cancel in Matching Pairs
blocks.text: Imagine a row of colored dominoes, where any two ADJACENT dominoes of the exact same color instantly vanish together, closing the gap between whatever was on either side of them. If that closing brings two dominoes of the same color together, THEY also vanish, and this cascading effect continues until no two adjacent dominoes share a color anymore.

blocks.caption: Each new character either cancels the stack's current top (if matching) or gets pushed on top (if not), automatically handling any cascade

blocks.text: Before repeatedly scanning the string from scratch after each removal (slow, and awkward to reason about cascades), notice that a stack naturally handles cascading cancellations in a SINGLE linear pass, since whatever survives just below a cancelled pair automatically becomes the new "current top" to compare against.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Walking through the string left to right, maintaining a stack of "surviving so far" characters, each new character either matches the stack's current top (triggering a cancellation) or does not (surviving, for now, pushed onto the stack).

Observation 2: The moment a cancellation happens (popping the matching top), the NEW top of the stack is now directly adjacent to whatever character comes NEXT in the string, exactly capturing the "closing the gap" effect of a cascade.

Observation 3: This means cascading cancellations are handled AUTOMATICALLY, without any special extra logic: a single linear pass with this push-or-pop rule is enough.

Observation 4: The final stack (read from bottom to top) is exactly the fully cascaded result string.
This is a direct stack-based simulation: push characters that do not match the current top, pop (cancel) when they do, automatically handling any cascading removals in a single linear pass.
Repeatedly scan the string for the first adjacent equal pair, remove it, and restart the scan from the beginning, continuing until a full scan finds nothing left to remove.

items: Scan the string for the first index where two adjacent characters are equal.
Remove that pair and restart scanning from the beginning (since the removal may have created a new adjacent pair anywhere), repeating until no pair is found.

codes.python:
def remove_duplicates(s):
    changed = True
    while changed:                                                          # keep repeating until a full pass finds nothing to remove
        changed = False
        i = 0
        while i < len(s) - 1:
            if s[i] == s[i + 1]:                                            # found an adjacent duplicate pair
                s = s[:i] + s[i + 2:]                                       # remove both characters
                changed = True
                break
            i += 1
    return s


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(remove_duplicates("abbaca"))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Restarting the scan after each removal correctly handles cascading pairs, since the removal could have created a new adjacent pair anywhere in the string, not just near where the removal happened.
This directly reflects the problem's definition, but is inefficient, redoing a full scan after every single removal.

blocks.text: Eventually removes every cascading pair correctly, since it restarts scanning after each removal, guaranteeing no cascade is ever missed.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n^2) in the worst case, since each removal can require rescanning a large portion of the string.
Space: O(n), for the string being repeatedly modified.
Limitation: repeatedly rescanning is unnecessary; a stack-based single pass achieves the identical fully-cascaded result in O(n) time.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force rescans the whole string after every single removal. Instead, use a stack: walk through the string once, and for each character, check if it matches the stack's current top. If so, pop (cancel the pair); if not, push the character onto the stack. Since popping exposes whatever was just below as the new top, cascading cancellations are automatically handled by simply continuing this same single pass.

Walk through the string once with a stack. For each character c: if the stack is non-empty and its top equals c, pop (cancelling the pair); otherwise, push c. After the full pass, join the stack's contents (bottom to top) into the final result string.
Use a single stack pass: push non-matching characters, pop (cancel) matching ones, automatically handling any cascade.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single linear pass.
Space: O(n), for the stack in the worst case.

When two characters cancel (are popped), the new top of the stack becomes directly "adjacent" (in the surviving result so far) to whatever character comes next in the original string, exactly mirroring what a physical cascade would produce. Since this check happens naturally on every subsequent character processed, cascading cancellations are resolved automatically, with no special-case logic or restarted scans needed.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["The new character matches the stack's top","Pop (cancel the pair), potentially exposing a DIFFERENT top that the NEXT character might also match (a cascade)"],["The new character does not match the top (or the stack is empty)","Push it, becoming the new top for future comparisons"],["End of the string","The stack (bottom to top) is exactly the fully cascaded final result"]]}

items: Checking "stack is non-empty AND matches" before popping avoids errors on an empty stack.
The C++ version uses the string itself as the stack directly (push_back/pop_back/back), since a string already supports these operations efficiently.
The final result must be read in the correct order (bottom of stack to top), matching the original left-to-right character order of survivors.

items: Checking for a match without first confirming the stack is non-empty, causing an error when trying to read an empty stack's top.
Rescanning the string manually instead of trusting that a single stack pass already resolves every cascade correctly.
Building the result in the wrong order (forgetting the stack must be read bottom-to-top to preserve left-to-right character order).

items: Explicitly stating "a stack handles cascading cancellations automatically, since popping exposes the new adjacency" demonstrates the key insight clearly, rather than defaulting to a slower repeated-rescan approach.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Remove adjacent matching pairs, REPEATEDLY, until none remain (cascading)" points directly toward a stack-based single-pass simulation.

items: How would you extend this to remove adjacent DUPLICATES of exactly k occurrences (not just 2)? Track a count alongside each stack entry, incrementing on a match and popping only when the count reaches k (this is exactly Remove All Adjacent Duplicates in String II, a related follow-up problem).

Why is the final result guaranteed to be unique, regardless of removal order? Because cancelling ANY adjacent equal pair is a locally confluent operation: the order of cancellations does not affect the final fully-reduced result, a property this problem's guarantee relies on.

How would you verify your stack-based solution handles cascades correctly? Trace an example specifically designed to require multiple cascading levels, like "abccba", confirming it fully collapses to an empty string.

The foundational "stack handles cascading cancellation" pattern, directly extended with a count-based variant in the related "k occurrences" follow-up problem, and conceptually similar to Valid Parentheses' matching logic elsewhere in this category.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n^2) time, O(n) space.
Optimized (single stack pass): O(n) time, O(n) space.

items: Pattern: Stack-based cascading cancellation
Core Idea: Push each character unless it matches the stack's current top, in which case pop (cancel); this automatically resolves any cascading removals in a single pass
Time: O(n)
Space: O(n)
Most Important Observation: Popping a cancelled pair exposes whatever survives just below it as the new "adjacent" character, automatically propagating any cascade
Interview Difficulty: Easy
One-line memory trick: Match the top: pop (cancel). No match: push. Read the final stack bottom-to-top
